title: Hong Shao Rou
subtitle: red-braised pork belly in soy, Shaoxing wine, and rock sugar
excerpt: Hong shao rou is Mao's favourite dish and a cornerstone of Chinese home cooking: thick slabs of pork belly braised for two hours in soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, and rock sugar until the fat melts and the skin turns lacquer-red. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Red-braised pork (红烧肉, hóng shāo ròu) appears in regional variations across China, with the most famous versions from Hunan and Shanghai. The dish was reportedly Chairman Mao's favourite food, which he ate at his home village of Shaoshan. Lin Yutang, The Chinese Theory of Art (and his cookbook notes), and later Fuchsia Dunlop, Every Grain of Rice (2012), document the Hunan village version. The Shanghai version (called Dongpo pork in another form) predates the Republican era and is traced to the Song-dynasty poet Su Dongpo.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the cooked pork in its braising liquid. Defrost overnight and reheat gently, adding a splash of water if the sauce is too thick.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well in a large casserole. The sauce thickens more when reduced at the end - watch carefully.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Improves overnight. Make up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate; reheat over a low heat. The fat can be skimmed once chilled.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Chinese rice wine used extensively in cooking. It has a dry, nutty flavour and is essential to red braises, stir-fries, and marinades. Dry sherry is the closest substitute but Shaoxing wine is widely available in Asian supermarkets and is inexpensive.

Crystallised cane sugar sold in irregular lumps, used in Chinese braising to add sweetness and a deep gloss to the sauce. Breaks down slowly in liquid. Available in Asian supermarkets. Soft light brown sugar is an adequate substitute.

content.text: Hong shao rou takes two hours but almost all of that is hands-off braising. The dish serves four and produces a sauce so glossy and rich it barely needs rice , though rice is mandatory. The key steps are blanching the pork to remove scum, then caramelising
before adding the pork to build a lacquered finish.
Buy pork belly with skin on. The skin is what becomes gelatinous and trembling after the long braise , skinless belly is a different dish.
provides the base liquid and a savoury depth that water alone cannot match.

items.prepNote: tied in a knot or cut into lengths

content.text: Put the pork belly cubes in a saucepan, cover with cold water, and bring to the boil. Blanch for 5 minutes, skimming the grey foam. Drain, rinse under cold water, and pat dry.

Heat {{vegetable-oil}} of oil in a Dutch oven or wide heavy pan over a medium heat. Add the rock sugar and let it melt without stirring, then swirl the pan and cook for about 2 minutes until amber and lightly caramelised. Watch carefully , it burns fast.
Add the pork cubes and turn to coat in the caramel. Raise the heat and fry for 3 minutes until the pork is tinged with colour on all sides.

Pour in the Shaoxing wine and let it sizzle and reduce for 1 minute. Add the dark soy sauce, light soy sauce, ginger, spring onions, star anise, and cinnamon. Pour in the boiling water , it should come about three-quarters of the way up the pork.
Bring to a simmer, cover with a lid, and cook on the lowest heat for 90 minutes, turning the pork every 30 minutes. The skin should be completely soft when pressed.

Remove the lid and raise the heat to medium-high. Reduce the sauce, turning the pork frequently, for 10 to 15 minutes until it is thick and lacquered and coats the pork in a dark glaze. Serve over steamed rice.

items.symptom: Pork skin is chewy rather than soft
items.fix: The skin needs a full 90 minutes on a low heat. If it is still firm after 90 minutes, add a splash more water and braise for another 20 to 30 minutes.

items.cause: Soy sauce brands vary in saltiness, or sauce over-reduced
items.fix: Add a small splash of water and reduce again more carefully. Taste before the final reduction and add a little more rock sugar to balance.

items.cause: Heat too high when melting rock sugar
items.fix: Use a medium heat and watch closely. Once the sugar turns amber, add the pork immediately as it will continue cooking from residual heat.

content.text: Hong shao rou is home food across China, with regional versions in Hunan, Zhejiang, and Shanghai. The Hunan version is spicier and uses more chilli; the Shanghai version is sweeter and sometimes adds hard-boiled eggs to braise in the sauce. Served at Chinese New Year and at everyday family tables in equal measure.
